descriptor_candidates.name: confinement_volume_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: H1: In pure-silica zeolites at infinite dilution, the fraction of gas-phase entropy lost (entropy loss/R) increases with the ratio of adsorbate van der Waals volume to accessible framework free volume per unit cell scale, i.e., tighter volumetric packing of the guest in the host void increases entropy loss.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Known zeolite literature (occupiable volume V_occ, Dauenhauer/Abdelrahman) shows smaller free volume per guest increases rotational entropy loss. Here AV (specific pore volume per framework mass) is converted to a per-molecule comparable quantity through the framework density scale, giving a dimensionless packing proxy that couples guest size (Vol) with host void space (AV). Mechanism: confinement restricts rotational (and partly translational) modes.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If, in the training set within the declared regime, entropy loss/R does not increase (non-positive rank correlation or MAE of a monotone model worse than constant baseline) as Vol/(Vol + AV/density_ref) increases, H1 is falsified. Also falsified if the proxy consistency check (finite-difference in Vol at fixed framework inputs) shows no consistent entropy change direction.

scientific_test.proxy_assumptions: AV/density is assumed proportional to occupiable volume per adsorption site; density's physical unit is unresolved, so only the dimensionless combination relative to density_ref is used. Vol is molecular vdW volume, not free volume; the ratio is a confinement proxy, not an equality condition.
scientific_test.physical_interpretation: Increasing guest volume at fixed host voidage raises packing tightness; increasing accessible pore volume lowers confinement. The ratio is not a physically normalized free-volume fraction because mass normalization is modeled, not measured.

descriptor_candidates.name: rotational_fit_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: H2: Entropy loss/R increases with the mismatch between adsorbate rotational size (product of the two largest principal moments of inertia, proxying the helicopter-rotation cross-section) and the largest free sphere diameter of the framework; molecules whose rotational envelope barely fits the pore lose more rotational entropy.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Literature (R1E08, R1E17, R1E29) attributes framework-dependent entropy loss chiefly to lost rotational degrees of freedom: smaller pores obstruct helicopter rotations. The rotational partition function depends on the principal moments of inertia (known_relation), while the degree of obstruction is proxied by the ratio of molecular rotational scale to pore diameter. The log-log form encodes a power-law-like confinement response without fitted constants.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If entropy loss/R does not increase with this descriptor in the declared training regime (no positive association; or finite-difference in PMI2 at fixed lsd_f gives inconsistent sign), H2 is falsified. Also falsified if MAE with this descriptor added exceeds the 14-input baseline MAE.

scientific_test.proxy_assumptions: PMI2*PMI3 proxies the rotational cross-section relevant to pore obstruction; lsd_f proxies the limiting cage/channel diameter but is not an average cavity diameter, and q-ratio thresholds of one are not physical equality. Molecular rigidity and single-site adsorption at infinite dilution are assumed.
scientific_test.physical_interpretation: Larger moments of inertia mean a larger rotational envelope and larger gas-phase rotational entropy; a smaller lsd_f means tighter confinement. Their log-ratio measures rotational crowding, not a fitted fraction of lost degrees of freedom.

descriptor_candidates.name: planarity_path_constraint
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: H3: Entropy loss/R increases when a planar adsorbate must traverse a pore network whose free-sphere path (lsd_p) is barely larger than its largest free sphere (lsd_f); in that one-dimensional-diffusion regime, planar molecules lose more translational/orientational entropy than in well-connected large-cage networks.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Evidence distinguishes cage-like frameworks (large lsd_f, small lsd_f-lsd_p gap) from channel frameworks (R1E05, R1E08, R1E26) and notes planarity governs how molecules pack against pore walls (R1E07, R1E24). PBF measures deviation from a plane, not a minimum diameter; combining it with the lsd_p-lsd_f connectivity gap tests whether orientational constraints during pore traversal, a shape/connectivity coupling, explain residual entropy-loss variation.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If, within the training rows in the declared regime, entropy loss/R shows no positive association with this descriptor, or if replacing PBF by an unrelated descriptor yields equal MAE (indicating the planarity mechanism is not operative), H3 is falsified. Finite-difference in PBF at fixed lsd_p and lsd_f must give a consistent entropy-change direction, otherwise falsified.

scientific_test.proxy_assumptions: The lsd_p-lsd_f gap is a connectivity proxy: small gap means channel-like, constrained traversal; large gap means cage-like, more orientational freedom. scientific_test.physical_interpretation: Flatter molecules in channel-dominated frameworks can orient to reduce obstruction and may lose less entropy than inferred from size alone; the normalized ratio quantifies this coupling without asserting q_PBF equals a physical diameter ratio.

descriptor_candidates.name: rotational_volume_log_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: H1: At infinite dilution in pure-silica zeolites, entropy loss/R increases with the power-law ratio between the adsorbate's full rotational envelope (product of all three principal moments of inertia, which sets the classical rotational partition function) and the framework's two pore-geometry length scales (largest free sphere and largest free-sphere path); molecules whose rotational inertia grows faster than the framework pore sizes lose more rotational entropy.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: The rigid-rotor partition function depends on the product I_A * I_B * I_C (R2E08): larger moments mean larger gas-phase rotational entropy that can be lost when helicopter/cartwheel rotations are obstructed (R2E02, R2E07). Confinement severity is proxied by lsd_f and lsd_p, since smaller-pore frameworks show larger rotational entropy loss (R2E26, R2E28). The log-log form encodes a scale-free power-law response; both arguments are dimensionless products of median-normalized ratios, so no fitted constants or unit conversions are introduced.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Within training rows (all rows, since no sub-regime is declared), if entropy loss/R shows no positive association with this descriptor, or if finite-difference in any PMI at fixed lsd_f and lsd_p yields an inconsistent sign of the descriptor change while MAE does not improve over the 14-input baseline, H1 is falsified. Also falsified if adding this descriptor leaves MAE of entropy loss/R unchanged relative to baseline.

scientific_test.proxy_assumptions: PMI1*PMI2*PMI3 proxies the rotational partition-function scale; lsd_f and lsd_p are pore-geometry proxies that are not average cavity diameters, and their product is not a physical volume. Rotational loss is assumed framework-dominated at fixed molecule, consistent with R2E07. Rigid single-site adsorption at infinite dilution is assumed.
scientific_test.physical_interpretation: The numerator tracks molecular rotational entropy capacity; the denominator tracks geometric confinement on a log scale. The ratio of logs is a power-law exponent, not a physical equality threshold; q-ratio values of one carry no special physical meaning here.

descriptor_candidates.name: guest_host_packing_fraction
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: H2: Entropy loss/R increases with the fraction of dimensionless packing pressure, i.e., the ratio of the median-normalized adsorbate van der Waals volume to the sum of median-normalized guest volume and framework accessible pore volume per mass; frameworks with smaller accessible void per mass confine a given guest more tightly, increasing the fraction of gas-phase entropy lost.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Literature (R2E03, R2E06, R2E11, R2E13) establishes that the fraction of gas-phase entropy lost is a function of framework confinement, with occupiable volume as a single material descriptor: smaller occupiable volume yields larger rotational entropy loss. Here AV (specific accessible volume, cm^3/g) and Vol (molecular vdW volume, angstrom^3) are each independently normalized by their own positive median references, so the sum inside the parentheses adds two dimensionless quantities only. This differs from the rejected round-1 formula by avoiding any dimensional addition of raw quantities.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Within training rows in the low-AV regime (below the AV median, i.e., the most confined half), if entropy loss/R does not increase with this descriptor (non-positive rank association), or if the finite-difference in Vol at fixed framework inputs does not consistently increase the descriptor, H2 is falsified. Falsified as well if MAE of entropy loss/R with this descriptor added exceeds the 14-input baseline.

scientific_test.proxy_assumptions: q_Vol and q_AV are independently median-normalized dimensionless ratios; their sum is a model construct, not a physical free-volume fraction. AV is specific volume per framework mass, so AV/Vol is not molecular free volume; the descriptor only tests whether the normalized guest-to-host volume balance correlates with confinement entropy loss. The physical unit of density is avoided entirely.
scientific_test.physical_interpretation: Increasing guest volume at fixed host voidage raises the descriptor (tighter packing, more restricted motion); increasing accessible pore volume lowers it. The direction of association is a transfer hypothesis from aluminosilicate hydrocarbon data (R2E13) to pure-silica infinite-dilution systems, not an established law.

descriptor_candidates.name: span_pore_size_mismatch
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: H3: Entropy loss/R increases with the scale-free mismatch between the adsorbate's overall spatial extent (SPAN, radius enclosing all atoms about the center of mass) and the framework's free-sphere path diameter; molecules that are large relative to the diffusion path lose more translational and orientational entropy because positional and orientation freedom along the pore network is reduced.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Unlike PMI-based descriptors (rotation-dominated), SPAN captures overall molecular size relevant to translational confinement. The Sackur-Tetrode translational entropy scales with molecular mass/size (R2E09, R2E16), and confinement reduces accessible configurational space (R2E01, R2E19). lsd_p, the largest free-sphere path diameter, proxies the limiting traversal dimension distinct from the cage diameter lsd_f (R2E24 proxy caveat). The log-ratio of two independently normalized dimensionless quantities gives a power-law mismatch measure with no fitted constants.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Within training rows restricted to the lower half of lsd_p (constrained-path regime), if entropy loss/R shows no positive association with this descriptor, or if finite-difference in SPAN at fixed lsd_p yields an inconsistent descriptor direction, H3 is falsified. Falsified also if replacing SPAN with an unrelated size descriptor gives equal MAE, indicating no specific translational-shape mechanism, or if MAE exceeds the 14-input baseline.

scientific_test.proxy_assumptions: SPAN proxies molecular spatial extent relevant to translational confinement but is not a minimum molecular diameter; lsd_p proxies the limiting diffusion path, not an average channel width. SPAN and lsd_p are independently median-normalized, so a log(q_SPAN)/log(q_lsd_p) value of one does not imply physical equality of the two lengths. Infinite dilution and rigid frameworks are assumed; transfer from general translational-confinement arguments to this dataset is a hypothesis.
scientific_test.physical_interpretation: Larger molecular span at fixed path diameter means more restricted positional configurations and greater entropy loss; larger path diameter at fixed span relaxes the constraint. The mechanism is translational/configurational, deliberately distinct from the rotational (H1) and volumetric-packing (H2) mechanisms.

descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: H1: In pure-silica zeolites at infinite dilution, entropy loss/R decreases as the normalized gap between the largest free-sphere path diameter (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere diameter (lsd_f) grows relative to their sum; frameworks where the diffusion path is barely wider than the largest cage (small gap) force tighter orientational/translational constraints during pore traversal, so adsorbates lose a larger fraction of gas-phase entropy than in well-connected large-path frameworks.

This replacement is a pure framework-side bounded index in [0,1): it equals zero when lsd_p equals lsd_f (isolated-cage limit, minimal connectivity) and approaches one when the path is much wider than the cage (open-channel limit). Literature (R3E26, R3E12) reports larger entropy loss in smaller-pore, less-connected frameworks (FER vs FAU). This is a new dimensionless combination, not a copied relation.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Within training rows restricted to the lower half of lsd_f (most confined half), if entropy loss/R shows no negative rank association with this descriptor (i.e., loss does not decrease as the gap index grows), or if the finite-difference in lsd_p at fixed lsd_f does not consistently increase the descriptor while MAE of entropy loss/R does not improve on the 14-input baseline (after_mae_R = 0.5708), H1 is falsified. Rigid frameworks and single-molecule infinite dilution are assumed.

However, performing experiments for many molecule-framework combinations is impractical. Computational experiments of adsorption therefore make for an attractive alternative. Nevertheless, there remain caveats. For example, quantifying the entropy using ab initio-based methods (such as density functional theory) is computationally demanding $ ^{18-22} $ or relies on approximations. $ ^{19} $ Such approximations include (1) limiting translation to the surface area of the zeolite, $ ^{23} $ which artificially restricts the entropy to a surface term; (2) invocation of the “harmonic approximation” based on the assumption of a very strong fluid–solid interaction that renders translations and rotations unimportant; or (3) employing the hindered translator/rotor model. $ ^{24} $ On the other hand, (classical) Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics simulations have proven successful in accurately calculating the adsorption entropy, $ ^{25} $ with the primary limitation being the number of force fields available to accurately model the adsorbate–adsorbent interaction. Although these simulations are numerically cleaner compared to experiment because they involve analyzing efficiently a greater number of molecule–zeolite combinations, it remains overwhelming to apply them to the millions of hypothetical frameworks. Novel topology-based, data-driven approaches have been shown to be adequate in predicting specific features such as adsorption capacity $ ^{6} $ and selectivity. $ ^{26} $ However, there are currently no similar models for entropy.

Molecular dynamics simulations showed that diffusion of 2-MeC6 in MCM-22 (between 450 and 850 K) in the sinusoidal 10-MR channels does not occur to a significant extent. $ ^{67} $ That study also stated that interstage diffusion (in the short bridges that connect the neighboring supercages) does not happen (for n-C7 and 2-MeC6) until elevated temperatures so that molecules spend most of their time inside the cage. In an NMR study of xenon adsorption in zeolite MCM-22, it was found that, particularly at low coverage, xenon atoms predominantly prefer to locate inside the supercages. $ ^{68} $ During the discussions of infrared spectrometric (IR) results, $ ^{69} $ it was declared that the supercages constitute about 70% of the micropore volume, indicating that the majority of the adsorption phenomenon is happening there. This argument was strengthened by the modeling calculations. $ ^{70} $ The authors determined the adsorption isotherm of n-C6 and 3-MeC5 at various temperatures on ITQ-1, the pure silica analogue of MCM-22, and suggested that three out of four adsorbate molecules are located in the large cages and one molecule in the sinusoidal channel system, which is in agreement with the supremacy of adsorption inside the supercages. In summary, on the basis of supporting information from literature, adsorption of linear and singly branched molecules will be considered, occurring principally inside the supercages of MCM-22. As the adsorbed molecules, whether they are linear or branched, are confined in a closed space, i.e., the supercage, their losses in translational and vibrational degrees of freedom will be comparable. Differences in rotational freedom in the supercages of MCM-22 may have a substantial impact on the adsorption equilibrium. Once identified, the contributions of the modes to the partition function are replaced by the correct ones for translational or rotational motions.

retained.name: guest_host_packing_fraction
retained.hypothesis: H2: Entropy loss/R increases with the fraction of dimensionless packing pressure, i.e., the ratio of the median-normalized adsorbate van der Waals volume to the sum of median-normalized guest volume and framework accessible pore volume per mass; frameworks with smaller accessible void per mass confine a given guest more tightly, increasing the fraction of gas-phase entropy lost.

retained.name: path_cage_connectivity_gap
retained.hypothesis: H1: In pure-silica zeolites at infinite dilution, entropy loss/R decreases as the normalized gap between the largest free-sphere path diameter (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere diameter (lsd_f) grows relative to their sum; frameworks where the diffusion path is barely wider than the largest cage (small gap) force tighter orientational/translational constraints during pore traversal, so adsorbates lose a larger fraction of gas-phase entropy than in well-connected large-path frameworks.
